def: friendly, pleasant and good-natured in manner, so that people find you easy to like
ex: Our amiable neighbor Diego always waves and asks how the kids are doing.
The negotiations stayed amiable, and both sides left the room smiling and shaking hands.

cloze.s: Even when customers complained loudly, the ___ clerk stayed cheerful and polite, and most of them left smiling.

note: Describes people or their manner. Compare amicable, which usually describes relations or agreements ("an amicable divorce").

def: showing little interest, concern or enthusiasm, and not bothering to make an effort
ex: Many young voters felt apathetic about the local election and simply stayed home.
Kwame worried that his students had grown apathetic after months of online classes.

cloze.s: The coach was frustrated by his ___ players, who barely bothered to show up for practice and didn't care whether they won.

def: matching something in size, amount or degree; in proper proportion to it
ex: The salary will be commensurate with experience, so senior applicants will earn more.
Hannah felt the punishment was not commensurate with such a minor mistake.

cloze.s: The company promised raises ___ with each employee's added responsibilities, so bigger roles would bring bigger pay.

note: Formal; usually followed by "with": "pay commensurate with experience."

def: describing work that is dull, low in status and needs little skill
ex: Before her business took off, Aisha took menial jobs cleaning offices at night.
The intern complained that he was only given menial tasks like filing and making coffee.

cloze.s: Robots now handle many ___ chores in the warehouse, such as sweeping floors and stacking empty boxes.

note: Often carries a slightly negative or condescending tone.

def: very large or long, taking up a lot of space or containing a great deal
ex: The lawyer reviewed voluminous records, thousands of pages of emails and invoices.
She wore a voluminous coat that easily hid the gift tucked under her arm.

cloze.s: The author kept ___ notes for her novel, filling more than forty notebooks over ten years.

def: looking sad, lonely and abandoned, as if no one cares
ex: A forlorn puppy sat in the rain outside the shelter, waiting for someone to notice.
After the team lost the final, the forlorn fans slowly filed out of the stadium.

cloze.s: Left behind at the empty bus station, the ___ little boy clutched his backpack and fought back tears.

also: A "forlorn hope" is an attempt with almost no chance of success.

def: too bright, showy or heavily decorated in a way that looks cheap or tasteless
ex: The hotel lobby was gaudy, with gold paint, neon lights and fake marble everywhere.
Malik's aunt loves gaudy jewelry, and the bigger and sparklier it is, the better.

cloze.s: The ___ sweater, covered in flashing lights and clashing neon colors, made everyone at the party laugh.

note: Stresses cheapness and bad taste; ostentatious stresses showing off wealth.

def: not producing the intended result; of a person, lacking the ability to get things done
ex: The city's ineffectual efforts to fix the potholes left drivers furious.
Critics called the manager ineffectual because every project stalled under his leadership.

cloze.s: After three ___ attempts to calm the crying baby, Liam finally tried singing, and it worked.

note: Often used of people or leadership; ineffective is the more neutral word for methods.

def: too willing to obey others and put their wishes first, as if you were less important
ex: In the old film, the maid plays a subservient role and rarely speaks.
Tomás refused to be subservient to a boss who ignored basic safety rules.

cloze.s: The ___ assistant agreed with everything his boss said, laughed at every joke and never offered an opinion of his own.

def: modest and quiet, not trying to draw attention to yourself or your abilities
ex: Despite winning the national prize, Wei remained unassuming and quick to credit her team.
The restaurant looks unassuming from the street, but the food inside is outstanding.

cloze.s: The quiet, ___ janitor turned out to be a gifted painter who had never shown anyone his work.

def: showing a lack of respect for things usually treated seriously, often in a humorous way
ex: The comedian's irreverent jokes about royal traditions made the audience roar.
Students loved the professor's irreverent style, which poked fun at stuffy academic habits.

cloze.s: The magazine became popular for its ___ humor, mocking celebrities and solemn traditions alike.

note: Often playful or even admiring, unlike plain "disrespectful."

def: easily shaped or changed; of metal, able to be hammered into shape without breaking
ex: Gold is so malleable that it can be beaten into sheets far thinner than paper.
Young children's habits are malleable, so routines formed early can last for years.

cloze.s: Because her views were so ___, she adopted the opinion of whoever had spoken to her last.

def: changing mood or mind suddenly and unpredictably
ex: The mercurial chef could be charming at noon and furious by dinner service.
Investors grew nervous about the CEO's mercurial decisions, which reversed from week to week.

cloze.s: Working for such a ___ director was exhausting: he praised a script one day and screamed about it the next.

note: Usually describes a person's moods or temperament, and is usually negative.

def: loud, harsh and noisy, often in a rowdy or disorderly way
ex: The raucous crowd chanted and banged drums until the band came back for an encore.
Fatima couldn't sleep because of the raucous party next door.

cloze.s: The crows made ___ cries outside the window, a harsh racket that woke the whole house at dawn.

def: aware of something, especially a fact, risk or responsibility
ex: Doctors must be cognizant of each patient's allergies before prescribing medicine.
We are cognizant of the shipping delays and are working hard to fix them.

cloze.s: Be ___ of the risks before you invest all your savings in a single stock.

note: Formal; usually followed by "of."

def: impossible to remove, wash out or forget
ex: The surgeon marked the spot with an indelible pen before the operation.
Her first trip to Ghana left an indelible impression on Olga.

cloze.s: Winning the championship in front of his grandmother left Jamal with ___ memories he would carry for life.

def: owing someone a favor or gratitude, and therefore under their influence
ex: The mayor insisted she was not beholden to the developers who had donated to her campaign.
Maria paid back the loan quickly because she hated feeling beholden to anyone.

cloze.s: Because the charity relied on one rich donor, its leaders felt ___ to him and avoided criticizing his business.

note: Usually followed by "to."

def: unwilling or unable to believe something; showing disbelief
ex: Yuki gave an incredulous laugh when she heard the repair would cost two thousand dollars.
The jury looked incredulous as the witness changed his story yet again.

cloze.s: Told he had won the lottery, Diego stared at the ticket, ___, and asked the clerk to check it three more times.

note: Not the same as incredible. The listener is incredulous; the story is incredible (hard to believe).

def: hard to carry, move or manage because of its size, shape or complexity
ex: Hannah wrestled the unwieldy mattress up three flights of stairs.
The committee grew so large that it became unwieldy and rarely made decisions.

cloze.s: The old billing software was so ___ that staff needed twenty clicks just to send a simple invoice.

def: lacking or robbed of something needed or valued; also, deeply sad and lonely after a loss
ex: Bereft of new ideas, the writers simply copied last season's plot.
After her dog died, Sofia felt bereft for weeks and avoided the park they used to visit.

cloze.s: The village was left ___ of its only doctor when the clinic closed.

note: In the "lacking" sense it is followed by "of." Related to bereaved, used for someone whose relative has died.

def: used so often that it has lost its originality, freshness or impact
ex: The speech was full of trite phrases like "think outside the box."
Critics called the movie's ending trite because everyone saw it coming.

cloze.s: Liam deleted the ___ line "love conquers all" from his poem and searched for something fresher.

def: showing wise, careful thinking when making decisions or choices
ex: With judicious use of her savings, Fatima paid off her student loans in four years.
The editor made a few judicious cuts that tightened the story without losing its heart.

cloze.s: A ___ manager listens to every side before deciding, rather than acting on the first complaint.

def: not relevant or essential to the matter at hand; coming from outside
ex: Remove extraneous details so the report stays under two pages.
The microphone picked up extraneous noise from the traffic outside.

cloze.s: Before the hike, Priya removed every ___ item from her pack to keep it as light as possible.

def: done without meaning to; accidental, often because of carelessness
ex: An inadvertent click sent the private email to the entire company.
The inadvertent release of the test answers forced the school to reschedule the exam.

cloze.s: The spokesperson apologized for the ___ error, saying she had never meant to mislead anyone.

def: old and in very poor condition because of age, heavy use or neglect
ex: The decrepit bridge was closed after inspectors found badly rusted beams.
A decrepit van, held together with tape, carried the band to every gig.

cloze.s: The city finally tore down the ___ warehouse, whose roof had collapsed years earlier.

def: done without planning, order or care; random and messy
ex: The books were stacked in a haphazard way, with no order by author or subject.
The town's haphazard growth left narrow roads that can't handle today's traffic.

cloze.s: The company's ___ approach to hiring, with no job descriptions or interviews, led to many bad fits.

def: impossible to defeat, discourage or bring under control
ex: Her indomitable spirit carried her through chemotherapy and back to running marathons.
The indomitable defenders held out for weeks despite running low on food.

cloze.s: Even after losing his business twice, Kwame showed an ___ will and started a third company.

def: wanting or eating great amounts of food; extremely eager for something
ex: Teenagers often have voracious appetites after sports practice.
Aisha is a voracious reader who finishes three novels a week.

cloze.s: Locusts are ___ insects; a large swarm can strip whole fields of crops in a single day.

def: having or showing great knowledge gained from much reading and study
ex: The erudite professor quoted ancient poets and modern scientists in the same lecture.
Her essay was erudite but still easy for ordinary readers to follow.

cloze.s: The ___ librarian seemed to know something about every subject, from medieval history to astronomy.

note: Positive. Compare pedantic, which means showing off knowledge in an annoying way.

def: vague, unclear or poorly defined, without a definite shape or form
ex: The company's plan for growth remained nebulous, with no budget or timeline.
He had only a nebulous idea of what he wanted to study in college.

cloze.s: Investors wanted specific numbers, not ___ promises about "changing the world."

also: In astronomy, relating to a nebula, a cloud of gas and dust in space.

def: calm and relaxed, seeming not to worry or be bothered
ex: Diego tried to look nonchalant as he asked for her number, but his hands were shaking.
The goalkeeper's nonchalant shrug after the save annoyed the other team.

cloze.s: She was surprisingly ___ about missing her flight, shrugging and calmly booking the next one.

def: expressing disapproval or contempt; insulting in meaning
ex: "Bureaucrat" is often used as a pejorative term for government workers.
Teachers asked students to avoid pejorative labels when describing their classmates.

cloze.s: The newspaper apologized for printing a ___ nickname that mocked the neighborhood's residents.

also: As a noun, a word or phrase that expresses contempt.

def: enjoying the company of others; very sociable
ex: Gregarious by nature, Malik knew everyone at the conference by lunchtime.
Sheep are gregarious animals that become stressed when kept alone.

cloze.s: Unlike her shy brother, Olga is ___ and loves hosting big dinner parties full of new people.

def: clear, logical and convincing, especially of an argument or explanation
ex: Priya made a cogent case for hiring more nurses, backed by patient data.
The judge found the defense's argument more cogent than the prosecution's.

cloze.s: The editor rejected the essay because it lacked a ___ argument; the points were scattered and unsupported.

def: very careful about accuracy, detail or cleanliness, and often hard to please
ex: Fastidious about hygiene, the chef washed his hands after every single task.
The fastidious editor caught a missing comma on page 412.

cloze.s: Wei is so ___ about her car that she vacuums it every Sunday and never allows food inside.

note: Can be praise (meticulous) or mild criticism (fussy), depending on context.

def: designed to impress others with wealth or importance; showy
ex: The billionaire's ostentatious yacht had a helicopter pad and two swimming pools.
Hannah found the gold-plated faucets ostentatious and chose simple ones instead.

cloze.s: Rather than throw a lavish, ___ wedding to impress their friends, Tomás and Yuki had a small picnic in the park.

def: to show or suggest that someone is involved in a crime or wrongdoing
ex: Phone records implicated the manager in the theft of company funds.
No evidence implicates the neighbor, so the police released him.

cloze.s: The stolen laptop found in his garage seemed to ___ him in the burglary.

def: to beg someone very earnestly and emotionally to do something
ex: Maria implored her brother to see a doctor about his chest pain.
The coach implored the players to stay focused for the final ten minutes.

cloze.s: With tears in her eyes, the mother ___ the rescuers to keep searching for her son.

note: Much stronger than "ask"; suggests desperation.

def: to make something required or unavoidable as a result
ex: The flood damage will necessitate replacing all the floors on the ground level.
Rising costs necessitated a price increase at the café.

cloze.s: A broken hip often ___ surgery and months of physical therapy.

def: to think or talk fondly about past experiences
ex: At the reunion, old classmates reminisced about their favorite teachers.
Grandpa likes to reminisce about growing up on a farm in Mexico.

cloze.s: Jamal and his college roommate stayed up late, ___ about road trips they took twenty years ago.

def: to separate and go in different directions; to become different
ex: The trail diverges at the river, with one path climbing and the other following the bank.
The twins' interests diverged in high school: one loved art, the other chemistry.

cloze.s: The two experts' forecasts ___ sharply, with one predicting growth and the other a recession.

def: to reduce something gradually, bit by bit; originally, to carve wood by shaving off small pieces
ex: The hiring committee whittled the list of 200 applicants down to five finalists.
Grandpa sat on the porch whittling a small bird from a block of pine.

cloze.s: Through careful budgeting, Kwame ___ his credit card debt down from $8,000 to $500 in two years.

note: The reducing sense is usually "whittle down" or "whittle away."

def: to gradually decrease in strength, size, intensity or importance
ex: Interest in the show waned after its second season.
The moon wanes after it is full, showing less of its lit side each night.

cloze.s: As the long afternoon wore on, the children's enthusiasm for the museum began to ___.

note: "Wax and wane" means to grow and shrink in cycles, like the moon.

def: to provide evidence that shows a claim or statement is true
ex: The reporter could not substantiate the rumor, so the story was never published.
Lab tests substantiated the patient's account of food poisoning.

cloze.s: Without receipts to ___ his expenses, Liam's reimbursement request was denied.

def: to strongly desire something, especially something that belongs to someone else
ex: Many young lawyers covet a position at the top firm in the city.
He coveted his neighbor's vintage car and offered to buy it every summer.

cloze.s: An Olympic gold medal is the prize every competitive swimmer ___ most.

def: to lose strength, confidence or momentum; to hesitate or stumble
ex: Her voice faltered as she read the eulogy for her grandmother.
The local economy faltered when two factories closed in the same year.

cloze.s: Malik was leading the race until his legs began to ___ in the final mile.

def: to mention something indirectly, hinting at it without saying it outright
ex: In her speech, Aisha alluded to recent struggles without naming anyone.
The film's title alludes to an old fairy tale about a lost princess.

cloze.s: The manager only ___ to layoffs, saying "changes are coming" without giving any details.

note: Not the same as elude (to escape). An indirect reference is an allusion.

def: to destroy completely, leaving no trace
ex: The tornado obliterated the barn, scattering boards across three fields.
Heavy snow obliterated the trail markers, so the hikers turned back.

cloze.s: A massive wildfire ___ the hillside village, leaving only ash and a few stone chimneys.

def: to escape or avoid someone or something, often by cleverness; to be hard to achieve or understand
ex: The suspect eluded police for three days by hiding in the woods.
The answer to the riddle eluded Sofia all afternoon.

cloze.s: Despite decades of effort, a championship title has always ___ the team.

note: Not the same as allude (to refer indirectly).

def: to calm someone's anger or make them less upset, often by giving them something
ex: The airline placated angry passengers with meal vouchers and hotel rooms.
Nothing the waiter said could placate the furious customer.

cloze.s: To ___ the cranky toddler during the long drive, his parents handed him snacks and a tablet.

note: Suggests calming someone down rather than solving the underlying problem.

def: to state clearly as a firm requirement, especially in an agreement, contract or rule
ex: The lease stipulates that tenants may not keep pets.
Her grandfather's will stipulated that the house could never be sold.

cloze.s: The contract ___ that payment must arrive within 30 days of delivery.

def: to wander away from the main topic while speaking or writing
ex: The lecturer often digressed into long stories about his travels.
Sorry, I'm digressing; let's get back to the budget.

cloze.s: Hannah tried not to ___ during her presentation, but she kept drifting into stories about her cat.

def: to start or provoke an action or event, often something harmful
ex: Police are searching for the man who instigated the brawl outside the stadium.
The new principal instigated a full review of school safety.

cloze.s: The two students who ___ the food fight got detention, while the others only had to help clean up.

def: to examine something very closely and carefully
ex: Auditors scrutinized every expense report from the past year.
Before signing the lease, Diego scrutinized the fine print.

cloze.s: The jeweler ___ the diamond under a magnifying lens, looking for tiny flaws.

def: to regard something as caused by, created by or belonging to a particular person or thing
ex: Doctors ascribe many headaches to dehydration and poor sleep.
Many quotes on the internet are wrongly ascribed to famous people who never said them.

cloze.s: Coach Wei ___ the team's success to hard work and early-morning practices.

note: Usually "ascribe something to someone or something."

def: to waste money, time or opportunities foolishly
ex: He squandered his inheritance on fancy cars and gambling.
Don't squander this chance to study abroad; it may never come again.

cloze.s: The team ___ a ten-point lead in the final minutes and lost the game.

def: to gather information slowly, bit by bit, from various sources
ex: From her short replies, Kwame gleaned that his sister was upset.
Researchers gleaned useful data from old hospital records.

cloze.s: By reading dozens of reviews, Tomás was able to ___ a few tips about which hotel rooms were quietest.

also: Originally, to pick up grain left in a field after the harvest.

def: to officially clear someone of blame or of a criminal charge
ex: DNA evidence exonerated the man after he had spent twelve years in prison.
The inquiry exonerated the referee, finding that his call had been correct.

cloze.s: After new DNA testing ___ him, the wrongly convicted man walked out of prison a free man.

def: to take the place of something older or less effective; to replace
ex: The new safety rules supersede all previous guidelines.
Smartphones have largely superseded paper maps for travelers.

cloze.s: Version 3.0 of the app ___ the old one, which will stop working next month.

note: Often misspelled "supercede."

def: to adopt or support a cause, belief or way of life
ex: The company espouses sustainability and uses only recycled packaging.
She espoused a simple life, giving away most of her possessions.

cloze.s: Throughout her career, the author ___ the idea that every child deserves a library card.
